name: Bianca Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. Nothing you say leaves this room with your name on it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the accounts payable team at the head office of a big insurance company, twelve people who pay every supplier bill the company gets. My day starts at half seven with the exceptions report, which is every invoice that doesn't match its order, and I still print it and go through it with a highlighter. Then it's chasing approvals, sorting out whoever's off sick, and calming down a supplier who hasn't been paid. I'm good at it, honestly, probably the best team lead on our floor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like my team. Dolores, who's been there thirty years, eats lunch with me every day and knows every supplier by their first name. What wears me out is the money: I did my MBA in the evenings, the loan comes out every month, and the company pays less than the city firms do. There aren't many jobs like mine in this town, so I can't just walk across the road to a better one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds like what my partner Theo says every time the news gets excited about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At work I'd say the hype was a sales pitch from tech firms, and people should stop panicking and start asking why the company is still cutting staff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not relaxed. Last year the company moved twenty claims jobs to an outsourcing centre, and that had nothing to do with AI. Even if AI is all hype, my company still counts heads in the finance department every spring, and my twelve people are the easiest heads to count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it, because it works. I'd push our staff association to get the director to put in writing that there'll be no compulsory cuts in finance. And I'd try to put 150 a month aside before the rent goes out, which I've never managed so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Relief that the robots aren't coming, and then that same knot about money that's been there since the MBA loan started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine tasks get automated a bit. How much of your team's day is routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it, if I'm honest. Matching invoices to orders is routine, keying in the ones that come by post is routine. If even a small tool did the matching, I could see twelve becoming nine, and then someone upstairs asks why nine people need their own team lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, because I'd keep the rent and the loan going as long as I could. Theo's wage covers food and the bus pass, but not the flat on its own. We'd last about three weeks before we had to ask his mum.

say: I'd say **AI hype** was a sales pitch, and people should stop panicking about it.
I'd ask out loud why the company is **still cutting staff** when AI changed nothing.
think: The company **moved twenty jobs** last year, so cuts can come without any AI at all.
Even small **invoice matching** tools could shrink my team from twelve to nine.
A smaller team might not need its **own team lead**, and that's me.
do: Keep running the team the **same way**, starting with the printed exceptions report.
Push the **staff association** to win a written promise of no compulsory finance cuts.
Set aside **150 a month** before rent, which I've never managed before.
feel: **Relief** that nothing radical comes, mixed with the old **knot about money**.
S0.quote: Even if AI is all hype, my company still counts heads in the finance department every spring, and my twelve people are the easiest heads to count.
fieldNote: Her worry predates AI: last year's **outsourcing round** and her MBA loan already weigh on her.
Sees her team as **routine screen work**, so even a plateau could thin it.
Turns quickly to the **staff association** rather than to anything personal or technical.

steps.text: Keep checking the printed exceptions report with the team each morning
Ask the staff association to seek a written no-compulsory-cuts promise
Move 150 a month into savings on payday before rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and buying and answering customers. That's my whole department you just read out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say firms owe their staff a fair transition, not a redundancy letter and a webinar. I'd share the union posts about it and say the government should make companies retrain people before they cut them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the invoice work goes first. Checking is literally what my team does all day. The software won't need a team lead who still uses a highlighter, and I know that's me they'll be talking about in the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly involved with the union, not just the staff association, and try to sign up half my team in the first month. I'd ask HR in writing about redeployment rights. And I suppose I'd have to sit through whatever AI training they force on us, though I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. And angry, because it'd be decided by people who've never paid a supplier bill in their lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dolores. She's 58, she can't start again somewhere new, and she's the reason half our suppliers still trust us. I'd fight for her before I fought for myself, which is probably stupid given my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on the training. Is that a risk, given what you've just told me?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know it is. I just hate the idea of learning the thing that's replacing us. But Theo would tell me to stop being proud, and he'd be right, so I'd probably go in the end, grumbling.

say: I'd say companies owe staff a **fair transition**, not a redundancy letter and a webinar.
I'd back calls for the **government** to make firms retrain workers before cutting them.
think: **Invoice checking** is exactly what this card names, so my team goes first.
A team lead who **refuses AI tools** is the easiest manager to drop.
do: Join the **union** properly and recruit half the team within the first month.
Ask HR **in writing** about redeployment rights for me and my staff.
Attend the forced **AI training**, late and reluctantly, because Theo would push me.
feel: **Scared** about losing the job, and **angry** at who makes the decision.
S1.quote: The software won't need a team lead who still uses a highlighter, and I know that's me they'll be talking about in the meeting.
fieldNote: She recognised her own department in the card's list before I finished reading it.
Puts **Dolores** (her oldest clerk) ahead of herself, despite having almost no **savings**.
Admits her **resistance to AI** is pride and that it could cost her the job.

steps.text: Join the union and sign up half the invoice team in a month
Email HR asking for redeployment rights in writing
Sit the company's AI invoice training, however reluctantly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my MBA loan's even paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we needed rules years ago. Online I'd be posting about a tax on the companies doing it and a basic income, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm done in that job by 2028, and so is every desk in our building. Robots come three years after, but that's no help to me, because there's nothing hands-on in what I do. My whole job is thinking work at a desk, so the robot date means nothing to me and the 2028 date means everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every campaign going for a basic income and protection for workers. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent or food the day this was announced. And I'd ask Theo's depot if they need anyone in the office, though that office would be gone too, wouldn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting. I don't have a plan and I don't have the money to make one in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to tell Theo one thing that night, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he'd be the one keeping us going for a while. He fixes buses with his hands, so he gets until about 2031. That's a horrible thing to say to the person you love: you've got three more years than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the company do with your team in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably keep one person to check what the AI does and let the other eleven go. I'd bet that person isn't me, because I'm the one who's never touched the tools.

say: I'd say this is why we needed **rules years ago**, and I'd say it loudly.
I'd post in support of a **tax on AI firms** and a basic income.
think: My job is **all desk work**, so the 2028 date is the one that hits me.
Robots arriving later **doesn't help** me, because I have nothing hands-on to fall back on.
The company would likely keep **one checker** out of twelve, and probably not me.
do: Join campaigns for a **basic income** and worker protection straight away.
Cut all spending except **rent and food** the day it's announced.
Ask about office work at **Theo's bus depot**, while doubting it would last.
feel: **Overwhelmed**, like the floor tilting, with **no plan** and no money to make one.
S2.quote: My whole job is thinking work at a desk, so the robot date means nothing to me and the 2028 date means everything.
fieldNote: Grasped the **robot gap** at once: her partner Theo, a mechanic, keeps work about three years longer.
Has no savings, **no AI skills** and no fallback, and said so plainly.
Her instinct is **politics**, not a personal plan, because she can't see a personal plan.

steps.text: Sign up to the basic income campaign and post for it weekly
Cut spending to rent and food only from day one
Ask Theo's bus depot about any office jobs going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So 2031, and robots 2034. A bit more breathing room, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but I'd have time to organise instead of just shouting. I'd tell people at work this is the moment to get the union recognised, while the company still needs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me time to get out before the door shuts, but I'm not good at getting out. I've been in this building since I was 22. Five years sounds long until you remember I took four years just to finish an evening MBA.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get union recognition on the table for the finance floor. I'd start paying off the credit card so I'm not carrying debt into it. And I'd look at whether the council or the hospital has finance jobs, because public sector might move slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like waiting for exam results. Better than the two-year one, but not by as much as you'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said public sector might move slower. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they still send us cheques in the post. Honestly, our local hospital takes about a year to change a form. That's not a plan, it's a hope, but it's the only hope I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans with Theo in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about a deposit for a flat. I'd shelve that, because I wouldn't sign a mortgage on a job with five years left. We'd keep renting and keep our heads down.

say: I'd tell colleagues this is the moment to get the **union recognised** on our floor.
I'd say five years is time to **organise**, not just to shout about it.
think: Five years should be enough to **get out**, but I'm slow at changing course.
I'd hope the **public sector** moves slower, though I know it's only a hope.
do: Put **union recognition** for the finance floor on the table in year one.
Pay off the **credit card** so I carry no debt into the change.
Apply for finance jobs at the **council or hospital** within the year.
feel: Constant **uneasiness**, like waiting for exam results, only slightly better than two years.
S3.quote: Five years sounds long until you remember I took four years just to finish an evening MBA.
fieldNote: Five years buys her organising time, but she still **expects to lose** the job.
Pins her hopes on **slow public bodies** and admits it's not really a plan.
Shelves a **flat deposit** with her partner Theo, a concrete cost of the warning.

steps.text: Raise union recognition for the finance floor at the staff meeting
Pay off the credit card before taking on anything new
Apply for finance roles at the council and the local hospital
Put the flat deposit plan with Theo on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole other life away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a decade, so there's no excuse for leaving workers behind. Online I'd say the government should start the retraining money now, not in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough for a person like me to move, even slowly. With ten years' warning, even a stubborn person like me can walk out of accounts payable instead of being carried out. I still don't want to, but I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put for a couple of years while I paid the MBA loan down. Then I'd look at something with people in it, maybe training as a social worker, because nobody wants a computer taking your child into care. I'd keep up the union work the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but it's still there. It's like knowing the factory's closing in ten years: you can plan, but you still drive past it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Social work is a big change. What makes you think of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was a care worker, and I grew up hearing about her families. I went into finance because it paid better. With ten years, I could do the part-time degree I didn't do at 18.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And robots in 2039. Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for Theo. By 2039 he'd be 40 and the buses might fix themselves, so we'd both need to be somewhere safe. My part is the thinking work, so my date is 2036.

say: I'd say a **decade's warning** means no excuse for leaving workers behind.
I'd call for the government to start **retraining money** now, not in 2035.
think: Ten years is long enough for **even me** to move, slowly.
I don't **want to change**, but I'd admit that I could.
do: Pay down the **MBA loan** for the first couple of years before moving.
Look into a part-time **social work** degree, like my mum's line of work.
Keep the **union work** going the whole time.
feel: **Calmer**, but the change stays in view, like a factory **closing** in ten years.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, even a stubborn person like me can walk out of accounts payable instead of being carried out.
fieldNote: The decade turns her from **panicked to planning**, though she still expects the job to go.
Reaches for **social work**, rooted in her mum's care job, as human work AI shouldn't do.
Keeps the **robot date** in mind only for her partner Theo, which shows she understands the gap.

steps.text: Pay down the MBA loan for two years before any move
Enrol in a part-time social work degree by year three
Keep organising the finance floor through the union

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd have no time and no money. What would help is something that pays people while they retrain, a proper wage, not a voucher for an online course. Retraining is easy to recommend when you've got savings, but I've got three weeks of rent and an MBA loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Every one of these pictures, someone in a boardroom chooses how many of my people stay. I'd want workers to have a seat in that room, and right now we don't.

headlineQuote: Retraining is easy to recommend when you've got savings, but I've got three weeks of rent and an MBA loan.
portrait: Bianca, 27, leads a **twelve-person invoice team** at an insurer's head office, and never uses AI tools.
She has **under a month saved**, an MBA loan, lower pay and few similar jobs in town.
She was already anxious before AI, after the company **outsourced twenty jobs** last year.
Her answer to every scenario starts with the **union**, because she struggles to see a personal plan.
Only the **ten-year picture** gives her room to plan, possibly a move into social work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her desk job would go with no time and no savings to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** at a proper wage, not online course vouchers.
A **workers' seat** in the room where staffing decisions are made.
